name: Beta-lapachone (investigational medicine)
short: Related analogue infused in 42 cancer patients: anaemia 79%, possible methaemoglobinaemia. Beta-lapachone tablets, 8 healthy men: adverse events all mild. PSC trial: generally well tolerated.
text: Beta-lapachone is an ortho-naphthoquinone first isolated from the heartwood of Handroanthus impetiginosus that has been tested as an investigational medicine; these data are not for lapacho (pau d'arco) bark products. In a randomised, double-blind study in healthy male volunteers (8 on the active tablet, 3 on placebo, twice daily for 8 days), a newly developed beta-lapachone tablet was taken by mouth; no serious adverse events were reported, and all reported adverse events were mild. A separate first-in-human study describes the same coded product as a molecule derived from beta-lapachone and reports that it was well tolerated at single and repeated doses by mouth, while two other human studies, whose abstracts give no adverse-event data, describe it as a synthetic beta-lapachone and a clinical form of beta-lapachone. In a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in 21 people with primary sclerosing cholangitis (15 on beta-lapachone), the authors report it was generally well tolerated; the abstract gives no adverse-event numbers. A related compound, described as a beta-lapachone analogue and given by infusion to 42 people with advanced solid tumours on three schedules (the abstract gives the 2-hour length only at the maximum tolerated dose), had anaemia as its dose-limiting toxicity; the most common treatment-related adverse events were anaemia (79%), fatigue (45%), hypoxia (low blood oxygen, 33%), nausea and vomiting (17% each), and transient severe hypoxia, reflecting possible methaemoglobinaemia (a blood disorder that reduces oxygen delivery), occurred in 26%. These analogue data may not apply to beta-lapachone taken by mouth. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
